title: Event detection
problem: Derive motion from tracking coordinates, then combine physical measurements with rules to identify event candidates.
ideas: Control: close, low, slow and sustained
result: Physics supplies measurements. Event definitions supply thresholds and timing rules.
notes: Start with coordinates and timestamps in metres and seconds. Player–ball distance is the Euclidean distance. Backward finite differences give velocity from displacement divided by elapsed time, speed from the velocity magnitude, and acceleration from velocity change divided by elapsed time. Compute within periods, reject gaps and missing coordinates, and inspect noise because differencing magnifies it. Combine these derived features into explicit event definitions. The control example requires the same closest player within 2 m, ball height 0–2 m, and horizontal ball speed at most 3 m/s for at least 0.3 s at 10 Hz. Pass candidates connect different same-team stable control intervals through a complete ball trajectory with at least 3 m displacement within 4 s. Acceleration is a diagnostic idea for kicks or deflections, not a gate used by the current detector. Conservative low-speed control can miss fast dribbles, aerial control or one-touch play; slow dummies can still qualify. Tune and evaluate thresholds using independent video-reviewed labels; a physical rule is not event truth.

title: Who controls the ball?
problem: Identify the likely ball carrier between recorded events.
methods: Require sustained proximity, low ball speed and low ball height.
result: Highlighted carrier states; uncertain intervals remain unassigned.
notes: Control candidate: same nearest player within 2 m, ball height 0–2 m and horizontal ball speed ≤3 m/s for ≥0.3 s at native 10 Hz. Velocity comes from adjacent-frame displacement divided by valid elapsed time, within a period. Missing speed, height, coordinates or frame continuity break the evidence. Video synchronizes distance, speed and stable ownership. This conservative offline heuristic reduces flyovers and fast dummies but can miss fast dribbles, aerial control and one-touch play; slow dummies can still qualify. No validated accuracy claim. Half-speed playback.

title: When does a pass occur?
problem: Separate a pass from touches, ball transit and reception.
methods: Link same-team low-speed control intervals through continuous ball travel.
result: Release and reception candidates align with the physics traces.
notes: Actual player–ball distances, horizontal ball speed and ball height share the clip time axis. Same-player proximity within 2 m, height 0–2 m, speed ≤3 m/s and ≥0.3 s persistence define the control endpoints. Different same-team endpoints form a pass candidate only if the intervening ball trajectory is complete, crosses no period boundary, travels at least 3 m and spans no more than 4 s. Transit can exceed the control-speed threshold. Dashed arrow and endpoints are retrospective candidates, not reviewed event truth. Acceleration is not a detection gate.

title: Formation and position identification
problem: How can we describe team organization while players move and rotate?
result: Examples: formation assignments, angular signatures and change timelines
notes:
How can we describe team organization while players move and rotate?
Ideas: Team shape and phase-conditioned averages; Formation-template identification; Player roles and positional rotations; Role signatures from relative geometry; Persistent formation-change candidates; Substitutions and asymmetric shapes

title: Which formation best fits this shape?
problem: Infer organization from positions rather than the team sheet.
methods: Center each frame, match players to template slots, then compare RMS error.
result: Minimum assignment error selects 4-2-3-1 from the four candidate templates.
notes: Best residual example from defensive 30-second windows; ten outfield players, at least 50 qualifying frames each. Four fixed templates and Hungarian squared-distance assignment. Player labels are assigned template slots, not reviewed role truth. Raw versus centered covariance ellipses appear as a small inset. RMS error is not a formation probability; not elastic EFPI inference. Selected option C with explicit template matching. Subtract the ten outfield players’ team centroid separately in every qualifying frame, then orient attack consistently. Take coordinate-wise medians over the window. For each fixed template, the Hungarian algorithm finds a one-to-one assignment minimizing total squared Euclidean distance between the ten medians and ten template slots. Compare root mean squared assignment distance across all four candidates. Here 4-2-3-1 has 9.13 m RMS versus 10.37 m for 4-3-3. This is a geometric best fit among supplied candidates, not a validated formation label. The ellipses summarize dispersion; the dots used for matching are medians. The final board uses schematic role slots.

title: Which spatial signature describes a role?
problem: Distinguish players by where their teammates lie around them.
methods: Pleuler-inspired teammate counts across rotating 90° sectors.
result: Contrasting angular signatures for wide, central and attacking roles.
notes: Twenty-four attack-normalized headings; teammates only in the comparison. Sector geometry is not observed gaze or occlusion. Metadata roles label the examples, not frame-level ground truth. No real role-classifier performance is claimed; the notebook’s classifier training check remains synthetic.

title: Did the formation actually change?
problem: Separate persistent reorganization from transient shape changes.
methods: Compare defensive windows; confirm only persistent candidates.
result: The timeline distinguishes raw candidates, confirmed labels and gaps.
notes: Dominant timeline and before/after pitch views. Three consecutive available 30-second bins confirm a candidate; missing bins reset evidence, while the last confirmed state is retained. Gray windows are insufficient samples. No substitutions fall in this bounded sample. Differing candidates are not claimed to be verified formation changes.

title: Physical metrics
problem: How much did players move, and what physical capacities did they demonstrate?
result: Sample calculations and official provider definitions are labeled separately
notes:
How much did players move, and what physical capacities did they demonstrate?
Ideas: Distance and valid tracking exposure; High-speed and sprint distance; Sprint efforts and repeated intensity; Acceleration and braking; Time to high-speed running / sprint; PSV-99 and Peak Velocity

title: How much ground did one player cover?
problem: Measure movement volume without hiding missing intervals.
methods: Integrate speed only across valid consecutive intervals.
result: Cumulative distance is reported alongside the valid sample coverage.
notes: Same smoothing and contiguous-segment derivative rules as notebook 06. Cumulative distance uses mean endpoint speeds and observed elapsed time. Coverage is valid integration seconds divided by bounded sample duration. Extrapolated positions may still contribute; no full-match extrapolation.

title: Who accumulated high-intensity distance?
problem: Separate high-speed running from total movement volume.
methods: Integrate distances within explicitly defined speed bands.
result: Player comparison bars show HSR and sprint contributions.
notes: Main bars: HSR [20,25) and sprint [25,infinity) km/h. Small speed trace illustrates threshold-qualified intervals. Exact equality handling is a teaching convention. Compare exposure/coverage before interpreting player rankings; these are not full-match or official production totals.

title: How many sprint efforts qualified?
problem: Distinguish sustained sprint efforts from brief speed spikes.
methods: Threshold speed, minimum duration and an explicit gap rule.
result: Qualifying efforts are shaded and counted on the speed trace.
notes: Uses ≥25 km/h for at least one second, with no merging across gaps. Efforts are numbered on the trace; count comes from notebook 06. These are not exact SkillCorner production effort counts.

title: When does the player accelerate or brake?
problem: Describe speeding up and slowing down around an effort.
methods: Differentiate smoothed scalar speed within valid segments.
result: Positive bursts and braking intervals align with the speed trace.
notes: Large signed acceleration trace; small synchronized speed trace. This is not acceleration-vector magnitude, and highlighted positive/negative samples are not automatically production-qualified explosive efforts. Derivatives amplify noise; smoothing changes peaks.

title: How quickly does the player reach HSR?
problem: Measure the elapsed time from 9 to 20 km/h.
methods: Inspect and interpolate one continuous rising-speed trajectory.
result: The observed threshold-crossing interval is visible and labeled.
notes: Separate slide for 9→20 km/h. Shows fastest qualifying monotone crossing found by the notebook’s sample rule. Official SkillCorner Time to HSR uses additional explosive-acceleration qualification; this slide does not reproduce that production metric.

title: How quickly does the player reach sprint speed?
problem: Measure the elapsed time from 9 to 25 km/h.
methods: Inspect and interpolate one continuous rising-speed trajectory.
result: Time to sprint is distinct from the maximum speed reached.
notes: Separate slide for 9→25 km/h with its own actual trajectory. No official Time to Sprint or Top-3 metric is reconstructed; opportunity, qualification and filtering matter.

title: PSV-99: a robust speed-capacity proxy
problem: How can speed capacity be summarized without one noisy maximum?
methods: SkillCorner’s 99th percentile of physical activities above 15 km/h.
result: The published example contrasts an activity-based proxy with peak speed.
notes: Original chart from SkillCorner, Peak Velocity article, 11 June 2026. PSV-99 is described as the 99th percentile of physical activities over 15 km/h, not all frame speeds. This figure is supplied research/product communication, not our sample calculation. Retain original legend and axes.

title: Peak Velocity: absolute top-end speed
problem: What is the highest speed a player reliably reaches?
methods: SkillCorner’s validated maximum-speed processing.
result: The provider’s published validation compares Peak Velocity with ground truth.
notes: Original SkillCorner figure. Article reports correlation 0.96 / R² 0.92 when averaging each player’s top three metric values in the displayed validation. Do not generalize this validation to our smoothed sample maxima or to every competition.

title: Game modeling
problem: Which locations, options and game states create or prevent scoring opportunities?
result: Start with simpler models, then add interactions and learned value
notes:
Which locations, options and game states create or prevent scoring opportunities?
Ideas: Shot quality and location value; Control, interception and completion; Accessible and dangerous space; Off-ball options and run threat; Graphs and learned relational models; Possession value and tactical applications

title: How does context change a shot estimate?
problem: Location alone cannot describe the goalkeeper and defenders.
methods: Compare location-only and contextual logistic xG on the same shot.
result: The same real freeze frame receives two different held-out estimates.
notes: Actual out-of-fold predictions from notebook 07; no model used the example match during that fold’s training. Context includes goalkeeper distance/offset and defender geometry. Selected for model disagreement, not as evidence of aggregate improvement. Freeze-frame coverage is not continuous full tracking.

title: Does context improve xG discrimination?
problem: Test contextual features across held-out matches, not one example.
methods: Same five match-grouped folds for both logistic models.
result: ROC AUC rises from 0.744 to 0.780 on the shared eligible cohort.
notes: Location AUC 0.743879, 95% match-bootstrap interval [0.713895,0.774165]; contextual 0.779870 [0.749411,0.809066]. Paired difference 0.035990 [0.021778,0.051104]. 1,000 match resamples of existing out-of-fold predictions, without refitting. Training-only scaling. ROC is discrimination, not calibration.

title: Which completed moves increase location value?
problem: Value progression before a shot is taken.
methods: Fitted location xT; value a completed move by V(end)−V(start).
result: Actual completed passes gain or lose value on the fitted map.
notes: Main map: licensed fitted DataBallPy open-play grid; SkillCorner successful player-possession passes use release coordinates x_end/y_end and supplied reception coordinates. Attack-normalized 105 m x scaled to the model 106 m convention. Two highest positive and one highest negative gains are selected examples. Small inset: synthetic two-state fitting mechanics from notebook 08; not training the full grid on this sample. Source provenance JSON stores event IDs.

title: Who is closest to each patch of space?
problem: Build a transparent geometric control baseline.
methods: Voronoi regions from nearest-player distance.
result: Hard boundaries partition the pitch into nearest-player regions.
notes: Grid approximation to Voronoi on a real frame. Strength: simple and interpretable. Limitation: ignores player movement, ball travel and uncertainty.

title: How does movement shape spatial influence?
problem: Replace hard boundaries with smooth directional influence.
methods: Projected Gaussian player influence, aggregated by team.
result: A continuous team-influence surface reflects movement direction.
notes: Directional Gaussian teaching parameterization, not exact Fernández/Bornn covariance. Bounded team comparison is not calibrated possession probability. Velocity and covariance affect the surface; contribution is not causal importance.

title: Which team reaches a target sooner?
problem: Model the race to space rather than only proximity.
methods: Reaction/projection time and earliest team travel time.
result: The arrival-time score exposes contested and reachable regions.
notes: 0.7 s projection/reaction and 5 m/s travel baseline. No full ball-flight, acceleration optimization or competing interception-rate integration. Not the full Spearman model.

title: How do the control assumptions change the answer?
problem: Compare methods without changing the tracking situation.
methods: Voronoi, Gaussian and arrival-time baselines on identical frames.
result: The moving comparison makes each model’s different boundaries visible.
notes: Original synchronized comparison video. Scores are teaching outputs, not calibrated possession probabilities; parameter choices are stated in assets/videos/README.md. Sampled at 5 Hz with real-time playback.

methods: Published pass-flight and player-interception simulation.

title: Why represent football as a graph?
problem: Positions alone hide who relates to whom.
methods: Players and ball as nodes; relationships as edges.
result: A graph encodes interactions without relying on player row order.
notes: Original graph illustration from Bekkers, PyData London 2025. General representation explanation before EPV: player/ball nodes, player-player and player-ball relations, adjacency and global context. The picture is conceptual, not a trained prediction. Source URL and attribution in assets/references/bekkers/attribution.json.

title: What information should a graph carry?
problem: Describe players and game context in machine-readable form.
methods: Node feature vectors plus global match-state features.
result: The feature matrix captures geometry and context for every node.
notes: Original node/global-feature matrix from the linked keynote. This is a general feature menu; do not imply our independent workshop GNN includes every displayed velocity, acceleration or global feature. Its actual features are current-frame geometry and identity/context indicators, specified in notebook 16.

title: Which relationships can the model exchange information over?
problem: Choose which interactions a graph can represent.
methods: Edge attributes and an explicit adjacency structure.
result: Connectivity defines the available routes for relational information.
notes: Keynote adjacency matrix shows one documented team/ball connection configuration, not a unique universal GraphEPV topology. Edge features can describe distance, relative geometry and team relations; the actual workshop model uses 20 m radius edges plus ball links, not this matrix. The main visual combines original edge-feature and adjacency illustrations from the same keynote; both source files are retained and credited.

title: What does a graph neural network learn?
problem: Use player relationships to predict a task outcome.
methods: Shared message passing, graph pooling and a task-specific readout.
result: Relational representations become a prediction for the chosen task.
notes: Original Sahasrabudhe & Bekkers architecture image reused in the keynote, attributed to its authors. General GNN explanation: shared updates, permutation-invariant aggregation and task-specific output. This is not our independent 353-parameter teaching architecture. No standalone temporal-network/encoder slides are included.

title: How does the graph change as players move?
problem: A useful relationship at one instant may disappear at the next.
methods: Recompute 20 m player-radius edges on real tracking frames.
result: The video reveals changing spatial neighborhoods in actual play.
status: Dynamic spatial graph · not a temporal GNN
notes: Player-only real radius graph at native 10 Hz. The trained workshop graph additionally includes a ball node and ball links. Recomputing spatial edges over time is not itself a trained temporal network or learned attention.

title: Graph EPV: what exactly are we predicting?
problem: Turn a tracking state into a clearly defined future outcome.
methods: Bekkers: one frame graph; goal by the possession team within 10 s.
result: A scoring probability belongs to a stated team and time horizon.
notes: Published PyData London 2025 target uses World Cup PFF tracking and event-aligned goals, respecting team and period. Our notebook trains an independent frame GNN on SkillCorner with reconstructed, score-audited goal timing. It is not Bekkers’ CrystalGraph architecture/weights or a full action-decomposed EPV reproduction.

title: Does our graph model generalize to unseen matches?
problem: Evaluate predictions beyond the training matches.
methods: Match-level holdout; validation-only model selection and calibration.
result: AUC 0.843; AP 0.020—ranking improves, probability reliability is limited.
status:
Test: 3 matches, 16 positive states
Brier .003335 vs .003308 baseline
notes: 16 included matches total: 10 train, 3 validation, 3 test. Test has 4,846 sampled states and 16 positives, not 16 independent goals. AP baseline prevalence 0.00330. Log loss improves 0.02363→0.02158; Brier worsens 0.003308→0.003335. Model mean prediction 0.00858 versus test prevalence 0.00330. Goal timing is reconstructed and not video-verified. ROC and PR are actual saved notebook results; no temporal model was trained.

title: How do supplied pass values differ across events?
problem: Inspect provider estimates without mixing model definitions.
methods: Join supplied event-value fields to their tracking context.
result: Pass EPV changes identify events worth examining in context.

title: SoccerMap: score every possible passing location
problem: Predict a surface rather than one chosen pass endpoint.
methods: Fully convolutional network over spatial tracking feature channels.
result: The published model produces a field-wide pass-success surface.
notes: Original SoccerMap Figure 3, arXiv 2010.10202v1. Yellow/blue attacking/defending players, arrows are velocity, white circle is ball; original probability color scale retained. A CNN, not a GNN. This result is from the paper’s data/model, not our SkillCorner inference. Other heads can address pass selection and expected pass value.

title: DEFCON: credit defensive positioning
problem: Value prevention beyond tackles and interceptions.
methods: Graph-based action values and defender responsibility estimates.
result: Published defensive credits distribute value among involved defenders.
notes: Original DEFCON paper Figure 3, page 7. Two intercepted passes; color is defender responsibility and numeric text is assigned defensive credit. Credit follows the framework’s assumptions, not causal proof. Cropped figure only, no values changed. Not model inference on our sample; authors’ underlying club dataset is not public.

title: Counterattacks: will this attack reach the box?
problem: Predict counterattack success from team interactions.
methods: Graph classifiers trained on synchronized tracking and events.
result: The published example shows a 49.5% model estimate for box entry.
notes: Original Figure 5a from A Graph Neural Network deep-dive into successful counterattacks. Women’s-model example predicts ending in the opponent penalty box with probability 49.5%. This is the published event-frame task; do not mix with additional all-frame goal-label datasets in the repository. Not our local model output.

title: TacticAI: improve a corner-kick setup
problem: Support decisions about receivers and player positioning.
methods: Geometric graph learning with predictive and generative components.
result: The published example compares receiver probabilities before and after adjustment.
notes: Original TacticAI Figure 3 from arXiv 2310.10553v1. Corner adjustment and predicted receiver probabilities are authors’ results, not interventions proven to improve match outcomes. Pre/post tactical suggestions are not locally generated or trained on SkillCorner. Retain original figure labels and legend.

title: GenTac: forecast multiple plausible continuations
problem: Represent uncertainty about how play may develop.
methods: Diffusion-based multi-player trajectory generation and event prediction.
result: Published forecast samples imply a distribution of possible tactical outcomes.
status: Published preprint result · Rao et al.
notes: Original GenTac Figure 5 panel a, arXiv 2604.11786v1. Four-second history, 20 generated rollouts and resulting event distribution are from the paper. Cropped original panel, no probabilities changed. Not a workshop-trained forecast, not a standalone temporal-network architecture slide and not causal intervention evidence.

title: What would make these results trustworthy?
problem: Distinguish an explanatory example from a reliable model.
methods: Independent match splits; task-specific error and probability checks.
result: A useful result states its target, evidence, uncertainty and failure modes.
notes: Event detection needs reviewed timing-tolerant matching. Formation/role labels require tactical ground truth. Physical comparisons require exposure and preprocessing definitions. Probability models need calibration and rare-event baselines. Stress-test extrapolated tracking, missing data, attack direction and domain shift. Current slide diagram is conceptual, not an extra experiment.
